tagline: Git branches the **files**; Claude forks the **conversation**. They are orthogonal axes — neither creates the other.
summary: Two different things can be 'branched' while you work with Claude Code, and they live on **different axes**. Git branches and worktrees isolate the **filesystem**: which versions of which files are on disk. Claude forks (session forks, agent forks) isolate the **conversation**: which transcript the model is reasoning over. **Forking a conversation does not branch your git repo, and branching git does not fork your conversation.**

sections.heading: The filesystem axis
body: A **git branch** is a movable pointer into your repo's history — switching branches changes which file versions are checked out. A **git worktree** goes further: it checks a branch out into its **own directory**, so two branches can be worked on **simultaneously** without switching back and forth.

Claude Code leans on worktrees for **parallel agent work**: spawning an agent with **worktree isolation** gives it a separate checkout to edit, so its file changes can't collide with the parent's. The conversation didn't branch — the **directory** did.

sections.heading: The conversation axis
body: A **session fork** copies the transcript into a new session. An **agent fork** spawns a background copy of the agent with the conversation so far. Both produce a second, independent **line of reasoning** — and **neither touches a single file or git ref**.
Your working directory, staged changes, and current branch are **exactly the same** before and after a conversation fork. Only the transcript copied.

sections.heading: Combining the axes
body: Real isolation for risky work often wants **both**: fork the conversation (so the original line of reasoning is safe) **and** put the work in a worktree (so the original checkout is safe). Each axis protects a different thing — the **thinking** and the **files**.
This is what agent worktree isolation does in one move: a background agent (conversation axis) working in its own checkout (filesystem axis).

diagram.caption: One task, two independent isolation axes — pick either, or **combine them** for full isolation.

nodes.label: Risky work ahead
nodes.note: A refactor, an experiment, a destructive migration — something you may want to **walk away from cleanly**.

nodes.label: What needs protecting?
nodes.note: The **transcript** (your line of reasoning so far), the **files** (your working tree), or both.

nodes.label: Conversation axis: fork the session
nodes.note: The transcript is copied; the original conversation is a **safe restore point**. **Git state is completely untouched.**

nodes.label: Filesystem axis: branch / worktree
nodes.note: A branch (or a worktree directory) isolates **file changes**. **The conversation is completely untouched** — same transcript, same session.

nodes.label: Fully isolated
nodes.note: Forked conversation + separate worktree: abandoning the experiment costs **nothing on either axis**.

scenarios.title: Protect the **line of reasoning** only
scenarios.note: Fork the session and experiment freely in the copy. Your **git state never changed** — there is nothing to clean up on disk if you abandon it (except any file edits the experiment itself made!).

scenarios.title: Protect the **working tree** only
scenarios.note: Work on a branch or in a worktree. The **conversation is the same one** — if the experiment fails, the transcript still carries everything learned from it.

scenarios.title: Protect **both axes** for truly risky work
scenarios.note: Fork the conversation **and** use a worktree. This is what agent **worktree isolation** packages into one move.

misconceptions.myth: Forking my Claude session creates a git branch (or at least a stash) to go with it.
misconceptions.reality: A conversation fork copies the **transcript only**. Your git branch, working tree, and staged changes are **byte-for-byte identical** before and after.
misconceptions.why: Both operations are called 'forking/branching' and both are about 'trying something safely' — but they protect **different things**.

misconceptions.myth: If Claude works in a git worktree, it gets a separate conversation for that worktree.
misconceptions.reality: A worktree is **just a directory**. The conversation continues in the same transcript regardless of which directory the work happens in.
misconceptions.why: Worktree isolation is usually mentioned alongside agent spawning, so the two isolations blur together — but they're separate decisions.

misconceptions.myth: Abandoning a forked conversation also rolls back the file edits made during it.
misconceptions.reality: File edits are on the **filesystem axis** — they persist no matter what happens to any transcript. Rolling back files is git's job (or rewind's, when checkpointing is on).
misconceptions.why: The transcript *describes* the edits, so discarding it feels like discarding them. The disk doesn't read transcripts.
